THE DAILY METALS PULSE | SUNDAY, NOVEMBER 22
#Uranium #Silver #Gold #Copper 

Oil is the first price I’m checking when futures reopen. Brent settled at $92.57 on Friday. A tanker was hit in the Strait of Hormuz on Saturday, and Saudi stocks fell 2% on Sunday. A sustained rise in crude would push up miners’ diesel bills. For gold, I’m watching whether the same inflation worries push Treasury yields higher.

☢️ Uranium — COP31 ended Sunday without an overall climate deal. The separate pledge to at least triple global nuclear capacity by 2050 has 39 countries behind it. For uranium miners, the nearer-term question is what utilities will pay to secure fuel. Friday’s spot price was around $90/lb, compared with TradeTech’s October long-term indicator of $99/lb.

🔶 Copper — At around $5.47/lb on COMEX, copper has fallen far enough for some US stockpiles to start moving back across the Pacific. The Financial Times reported Saturday that the premium buyers are paying in China is more than twice the cost of shipping the metal from the US. I’ll be watching whether that premium holds as cargoes arrive.

📅 What I’m watching next week

Monday, Nov 23 — US and eurozone flash PMIs. Silver fell 16% last week to $41.08/oz on COMEX. The first number I’ll look for is new factory orders. A pickup would be encouraging for both silver and copper demand.

Wednesday, Nov 25 — US October PCE inflation and the second estimate of Q3 GDP land at 8:30 a.m. ET. Markets expect core inflation to rise 0.3% on the month. A softer reading that pulls the two-year Treasury yield lower would give gold a chance to recover from last week’s 9% slide to $3,539/oz.

Friday, Nov 27 — China reports October industrial profits. US stock markets close Thursday for Thanksgiving and at 1 p.m. ET on Friday, so I’ll be checking trading volume before reading much into a late-week move in the junior miners.

Follow @Swedish_Uranium for the next Daily Metals Pulse.

my review of the iPhone Duo so far after a few weeks:

- its a spiky experience. Tablet mode makes you feel like a king in bed, on the throne, while working. Makes me feel like I have a laptop with me anywhere. But as a phone, it’s not great

- it’s amazing to open it up as a tablet, pair it with a Bluetooth keyboard, lay it down on a table and start working away. Termius+Herdr. Email. Crazy convenient and somehow even though I also have a bunch of iPads, I still use it as my go-to

- in the new world where we spend so much time in CLIs and doing text prompting, you don’t need a crazy amount of screen space. So this is perfect

- at my desk I’ve gotten used to having my main laptop display, then attaching a keyboard while having it placing it on an Anker wireless charger stand, and use it almost as a second display

- I have work nooks in my home gym, kitchen, etc since if you stash a Bluetooth keyboard there you basically have a laptop stand. (Proto Arc and Keychron folding keyboards are great)

- as you’d expect, well built, hinge works great, etc. Heavy though.

- there’s some intriguing new UX ideas floating around - leaving the Duo partially folded, sitting like a mini laptop. Using the folding/unfolding as an action, etc. Curious where this all goes or if it’ll be a gimmick 

- It didn’t ship with face recognition to unlock and it was so annoying to rely on Touch ID i thought about returning it just because of the unlock experience. They’ve since added some variant of it back, and it’s much better

Some various complaints:

- the magnetic chargers work well with the Duo in phone mode, but when the tablet mode is in landscape, its too heavy and lopsided to be able to fit on most of the magnetic chargers

- there’s lots of catch up on wrt software. In phone mode, there’s no vertical space. Apps like slack show maybe a few lines of content when the keyboard is up? Tons of vertical space eaten by the keyboard suggestions, two-line input, etc. Almost unusable

- on the iPad, the multitasking features are great. Mouse support, command+tab app switching, etc. The Duo weirdly doesn’t have any of this stuff even though you really want it to, as a tablet

- if you put a bunch if iPhone apps and Duo screens side by side (like X, the Home Screen, etc) even though the display is much bigger it doesn’t actually fit that much more content. Instead things are kind of “zoomed in” as it’s mostly a bigger/better viewing experience. For things like X timelines you actually would like for it to feel like way more content and much more scannable

- I also have had various generations of the Samsung Fold series and they historically had a more traditional form factor when closed (longer, less square-like). Super interesting that Apple didn’t choose this as I’m not sure it comes with much drawbacks? The unfolded format is very similar

- typing is a little awkward given the size. you definitely need a little grip thing to handle it in tablet mode. I saw someone recommended the  Popsockets low-profile grip, and although its a little weirdly floppy to make it low profile, I’ve gotten used to it and it’s good. The stand it comes with is useful

- i haven’t noticed the difference on the camera and other things people have complained about

All in all, I think a great V1. Again, very spiky. I think as the overall software and UX paradigm advances, itll get much better as the hardware is well built and (besides the weight) really great

You got some things right and other things wrong, but in general, your overall construct is incorrect.  It is not the case that the other alts contributed all of their performance fees to their public companies, and that our shareholders don't benefit from the investment performance generated by our funds.  

It is true that Pershing Square Inc. ($PS) is structured differently from the other alternative asset managers (alts) like Blackstone, KKR, and others. Our unique structure is highly beneficial to our company and our shareholders, as I explain below.

In short, when Blackstone and the other alts went public, they contributed a substantial portion -- typically 40% to 60%, but not all of their incentive, performance, or promote compensation to the public company and retained the balance to compensate their employees.

The outcome of this approach has been suboptimal.  First, promote income, particularly from private equity funds, is highly volatile. It is only earned and paid when funds generate a return in excess of a preferred return and when a liquidity event happens, that is, when portfolio companies and/or the funds' real estate assets are sold. As a result, analysts and investors in the alts value the highly volatile income from incentive fees at a low multiple. 

Wall Street likes recurring and growing fee streams like management fees. It does not like volatile incentive fee income.

By contributing so much of their incentive fees to their public companies, the other alts did not retain enough incentive fees to pay their teams. The result is that the other alts grant large amounts of equity compensation to their employees in addition to the promote income they pay to their employees. This equity compensation dilutes reported earnings by as much as 20% or more.

In order to address these concerns, when we structured Pershing Square Inc. (PS) in anticipation of its public offering, we bifurcated the performance fee differently. Rather than giving Pershing Square Inc. a pro rata slice of our performance fees, we gave the public company a senior interest in our performance fee income -- what we call Preferred Performance Fees -- and employees retained a subordinate interest in the incentive fee income, what we call Subordinated Performance Fees. 

PS retains the performance fees on the first five percentage points of returns net of management fees from our funds that charge performance fees, and our employees receive the performance fees on returns above 5% if there are any.  

If our funds do not earn a return in excess of 5% in any year, any unpaid Preferred Performance Fees accrue into a future year or years until they are earned and paid.  In other words, the company and our shareholders get paid first before our employees.

As long as investors believe we can earn a gross compound return of 6.5% -- the 5% preferred return plus the 1.5% annual management fee -- over the long term (a high likelihood, in our view, in light of our investment strategy that has generated gross returns of nearly 20% for the last 23 years), Preferred Performance Fees are effectively economically equivalent to management fees and therefore deserving of a similar valuation multiple.

We believe our high-return investment strategy will allow us to not only earn the Preferred Performance Fees over time, but also enable us to continually earn Subordinate Performance Fees that we can use to compensate, recruit and retain high quality talent. As a result, we don't need to issue large amounts of stock and option compensation to employees like the other alternative investment managers, minimizing the risk of dilution to shareholders.

[PS also benefits from the fact that, as is typical in the hedge fund industry, we earn incentive fees from both realized and unrealized gains so we are not forced to sell assets in order to generate returns.  Our funds generate performance fees as long as our annual performance net of management fees is positive, which makes our performance fees much more recurring than those from private equity or private real estate funds.]

While in a great performance year, the amount of performance fees earned by Pershing Square Inc. is effectively capped by our structure, the growth in assets that occur from great performance years inure to the benefit of all shareholders in that year and in future years.  

For example, if, in one year, we generate 30% net returns, while PS only receives performance fees on the first five percentage points of return, its cash flows and intrinsic value grow substantially due to the net 30% increase in fee-paying assets that is generated from our investment performance.  

Because 98% of our capital is in permanent capital vehicles, nearly all of our net performance is continually reinvested and compounded in our funds and additive to the growth of our fee-paying assets in that year and in future years.

With respect to your claim that this structure creates a conflict, I disagree. 

First, the structure was clearly explained to all investors in the IPO and in our public filings, and investors and analysts have found the structure extremely favorable, particularly when compared with the other alts.  

Second, our structure incentivizes us to generate excellent investment returns and enables us to attract and retain the best talent without burdening the company with excess G&A, restricted stock or option expenses.

Third, any new funds we launch which generate performance fees will have the same Preferred Performance Fee structure and therefore benefit PS in the same manner as do our existing funds.  

Fourth, our employees own the substantial majority of our shares creating further alignment.  We own a greater percentage of our company than do the employees of any of the other alternative asset managers.

Fifth, since we have retained, effectively outside of the company, sufficient performance fee income to compensate, retain and recruit employees, we are able to manage PS with a relatively modest amount of general and administrative expense of about $50 million. This has enabled us to operate with the highest operating margins of any of the publicly traded alternative asset managers. 

Thank you for the taking the time to write your post, which has given me the opportunity to clarify the concerns that you raised.  

I welcome any further questions or concerns that you or other shareholders may have.

X for the win.

The only way to turn BlurPool ETH into regular ETH is to use `withdraw()`, which several contracts holding BlurPool (from royalties) do not implement. The only escape hatch for them was for Blur to upgrade the pool contract. Or at least, that WAS the only escape hatch.

Blur just executed a series of transactions to brick the Safe that owns Blur, Blend, and BlurPool. That means that finally, officially, Blur can never be upgraded.

I went through the ~125k Blur Pool holders. 889 of those are contracts, holding 1,216 ETH.

315 of those contracts are immutable and do not implement a `withdraw()`, and they hold a total of 545.6 ETH. There is no way for them to ever receive the ETH.

558 contracts hold 550.9 ETH that IS withdrawable, but hasn't been withdrawn yet.

2 contracts owned by Cool Cats owns 117.1 ETH and are unverified, but through decompilation I was able to uncover a generic fallback function that appears to be able to withdraw if passed the correct calldata.

Out of the locked ETH, the biggest locked bags:

• Moonbirds family (PROOF): 173.2 ETH. 
• Milady "One" vault: 85.0 ETH.
• 0xSplits SplitWallets: 82.6 ETH across 63 splits.
• Super PUMA 0x41197b…: 62.9 ETH. 
• Invisible Friends 26.5, Iron Paw Gang 21.2, loomlock 16, then a long tail of royalty splitters under 2 ETH each.

The lesson here is that royalty splitters, simple as they may seem, need to be equipped to handle the unexpected. Either a generic extcall or upgradeability are good solutions, of course with appropriate safety considerations.

Anyway, RIP blur. you will not be missed.

Cerebras loves to claim that their output interactivity is 2000 tok/s/user on Kimi K3.1 2.8T, but based on their demo (YouTube video “Cerebras Demo: Running Kimi K3.1 at 2,000 Tokens/Sec”), that is only for short contexts with a context prompt less than 100 tokens long.

Interesting that they don’t show their p99 TPOT at medium (100k+) to long contexts (600k+) on agentic multi-turn workloads, which would affect performance as they need to load the KV cache for all of the previous tokens in the context for Kimi K3.1 Pro’s Gated MLA layers (full attention).

Also somewhat misleading is that whenever they quote a GB300 NVL72, they quote it at the maximum power of 150kW per rack. Based on our GB300 experiments with Kimi K3.1 Pro on GB300 NVL72 low-latency megakernels, the measured all-in rack power is less than 30% of maximum power, as low latency is memory-bound.

We welcome Cerebras to demonstrate their claims on AgentX Preview if they are actually confident in them, as it tests all of the things that their marketing does not. We wonder what excuse (coping) they will give this time to avoid demonstrating their claims, considering the tests take less than a couple of hours and can be done during off-peak hours.

Jakub Pachocki, Chief Scientist at OpenAI, on the impending capabilities acceleration in 2027:

'We have recently witnessed unprecedented acceleration in another domain. For more than a year, we have been posing open problems in mathematics to our models as one of the ways of evaluating them. Once we upgraded to a model of log-perplexity ~0.76, it started producing groundbreaking results. For many of us that have previously worked in mathematics and adjacent fields, seeing the resolutions to questions we've long thought about coming out of the model one after another in a single Slack thread felt deeply surreal. Having experienced that allows us to extrapolate - such a sudden transformation is plausible in deep learning research too. While this field relies more on experimentation, there is a long history of simple insights being missed for years; and so as soon as 2027 we could conceivably see a similar avalanche of fundamental pretraining advancements.'

thread_tweets.text: Greg Brockman:
thread_tweets.quoted_tweet_text:
I helped start OpenAI because I want AGI to be safe and beneficial for people. This post provides transparency that can be the foundation of industry-wide shared safety bars.

Perhaps the most important concept from the post is the following: "AI will also significantly contribute to progress on alignment and monitoring, I think that progress is unlikely to be fast enough to allow the full potential acceleration in pretraining."

Towards ensuring that safety keeps pace with general intelligence of pretrained models (as measured by "perplexity"), the post proposes "common limits, based on perplexity and other measurements, that developers are committed to not crossing until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieves a certain concrete milestone (such as the development of a successor to CoT monitors)."

The general idea is to create a first shared limit, on some shared key metric, along with concrete exit criteria that would allow going beyond that. This can lead to a "common framework for setting successive limits and pacing further development".

Excited to move forward the conversation on pacing towards shared standards that are rooted in the science!
